sections.title: Basic Concept
sections.content: In Courses of Action questions, a problem is presented followed by several possible steps. We must determine which step can effectively solve the problem. At Level 2, the questions become slightly more analytical, and it becomes important to understand administrative procedures, balanced decision-making, and the combination of multiple actions.

sections.title: Administrative Procedures
sections.content: In government or institutional decisions, there is usually a defined procedure. Immediately dismissing an employee or punishing an organization without investigation is not considered a proper Course of Action. A more logical step is to first form an investigation committee, collect facts, and then make a decision.

sections.title: Proportionality (Balanced Response)
sections.content: The solution should be proportional to the problem. If the issue is small, an extremely harsh decision is considered incorrect. For example, if an accident occurs in an industry, permanently shutting down the entire industry would not be appropriate. Instead, strengthening safety regulations and increasing inspections would be a better solution.

sections.title: Multi-pronged Approaches
sections.content: In many situations, a problem is so large that it requires more than one step to solve it. Especially in natural disasters or social issues, multiple actions are necessary simultaneously. For example, during a flood situation, both sending people to safe places and establishing relief camps are necessary steps.

sections.title: Practicality and Resources
sections.content: A Course of Action should be feasible with the available resources. If a solution is extremely expensive, impossible, or excessively complicated, it is usually not considered correct. Therefore, real-world conditions and available resources must always be considered when choosing a solution.

sections.title: Focus on the Root Cause
sections.content: A good Course of Action addresses the root cause of the problem. Instead of only stopping the outcome, understanding and targeting the cause of the issue makes the solution more effective.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: Many students consider extremely harsh solutions as correct. Some ignore administrative procedures. Another common mistake is assuming that only one solution can be correct, while in many cases multiple actions may be required together.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Courses of Action questions, the solution should be related to the problem, practical, and balanced. Administrative procedures should be followed, and in many situations a combination of multiple actions may be correct.

tricks.title: Check the Procedure
tricks.explanation: If the question involves an administrative or government decision, check whether the proper procedure has been followed.
tricks.example: If an employee is accused, forming an investigation committee first is the appropriate step.

tricks.title: Identify Extremely Harsh Decisions
tricks.explanation: If the solution is excessively harsh compared to the problem, it is usually incorrect.
tricks.example: Closing an entire industry because of one accident is not appropriate.

tricks.title: Regulation vs Ban
tricks.explanation: In many situations, regulations and controls are better solutions than a complete ban.
tricks.example: Instead of shutting down a dangerous industry, strengthening safety rules.

tricks.title: Multiple Solutions May Exist
tricks.explanation: Many problems require several actions at the same time.
tricks.example: After an earthquake, sending rescue teams and establishing relief camps.

tricks.title: Attack the Cause
tricks.explanation: The solution should target the root cause of the problem.
tricks.example: If accidents occur due to poor roads, improving the road is the correct step.

tricks.title: Check Practicality
tricks.explanation: The solution should be realistic and implementable.
tricks.example: Building a metro immediately to solve traffic problems in a small city is not practical.

tricks.title: Eliminate Unrelated Actions
tricks.explanation: If a given action is not related to the problem, it can be eliminated immediately.
tricks.example: If the problem is pollution, organizing a sports competition is not a solution.

tricks.title: Identify Immediate and Long-term Solutions
tricks.explanation: Sometimes both immediate relief and permanent solutions can be correct.
tricks.example: During floods, sending people to safe places immediately and building dams for the future.

tricks.title: Choose Balanced Decisions
tricks.explanation: The best solution is neither too harsh nor too weak.
tricks.example: If there is a discipline problem in school, strengthening the rules.

tricks.title: Group-based Solutions
tricks.explanation: Large problems often require cooperation between multiple departments or groups.
tricks.example: During a natural disaster, police, administration, and medical teams work together for relief operations.
